entities.name: Church of Nigeria
entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
The Church of Nigeria (Anglican Communion), established as part of the Church Missionary Society's West African mission (founded in Nigeria from 1842) and formally organized as the Church of Nigeria in 1979 after separation from the Church of the Province of West Africa, is the largest Anglican church in the world — with approximately 18 million members (largest Anglican body outside the Church of England) and 161 dioceses, making it the most consequential province of the Anglican Communion in terms of membership and theological influence. Nigeria's Anglican growth reflects the broader African Christianity explosion.

The CMS first established a mission in Abeokuta (1842) following the return of freed Yoruba slaves from Sierra Leone. Samuel Ajayi Crowther — a Yoruba man taken as a slave, freed by the Royal Navy, and educated in Freetown — became the first African Anglican bishop in 1864 (Bishop of Western Equatorial Africa), the most significant milestone in African Anglican history. Nigerian Christianity grew explosively after independence (1960), with the church organizing as an independent province in 1979.

The Church of Nigeria under Archbishop Peter Akinola (2000-2010) became the center of Anglican Communion controversy over homosexuality: Akinola opposed the 2003 consecration of Gene Robinson (first openly gay Anglican bishop, in New Hampshire) and led the Global South Anglican movement that threatened to split the Anglican Communion. The Church of Nigeria adopted its own 'CANA' (Convocation of Anglicans in North America) to provide conservative alternative to The Episcopal Church in the US. Nigeria now sends missionaries to the West — reversing the 19th-century missionary direction.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: The Church of Nigeria — growing from a CMS mission in 1842 to the world's largest Anglican denomination in 180 years, and now sending missionaries to the former colonial powers — represents the most complete reversal of Christian missionary direction in modern history, and its role in the Anglican homosexuality controversy makes it the most consequential single church in contemporary ecumenical politics.
